limit-zero.title: Ratio equals zero
limit-zero.prompt: If lim f(n)/g(n)=0, which requested classification is correct?
limit-zero.hint: f becomes small relative to g.

help.concept: A zero ratio means f grows strictly slower, so f=O(g).

limit-rule.title: Classify Growth with the Ratio Limit
limit-rule.bodyMarkdown:
For positive functions, form the ratio

$$
L=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{f(n)}{g(n)}.
$$

Then interpret the result in the direction asked:

- If `L = 0`, then `f` grows strictly slower and `f(n) = O(g(n))`.
- If `0 < L < ∞`, the functions grow at the same asymptotic rate and `f(n) = Θ(g(n))`.
- If `L = ∞`, then `f` grows strictly faster and `f(n) = Ω(g(n))`.

The stronger little-o and little-omega statements also apply in the first and third cases, but the handout asks for `O`, `Ω`, or `Θ`.

### Direction matters

Always compute `f(n) / g(n)`, not whichever ratio looks easier. Reversing the ratio swaps the zero and infinity outcomes.

### Source clarification

On the handout’s refresher slide, the nearby “upper bound” and “lower bound” headings are visually paired with the opposite ratio outcomes. The equations show the intended standard rule above: ratio `0` gives `O`; ratio `∞` gives `Ω`.

limit-outcomes-animation.title: Three Possible Ratio Outcomes
limit-outcomes-animation.context: The position of the ratio determines which asymptotic statement is justified.

steps.title: Ratio tends to zero
steps.body: f becomes negligible compared with g. Report f = O(g).

steps.title: Ratio tends to a positive constant
steps.body: Neither function becomes negligible. They differ only by bounded constant factors.

steps.title: Ratio tends to infinity
steps.body: f dominates g. Report f = Ω(g).
